Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Caleb Vance was thirty-two when his body stopped cooperating. It began as a heavy pressure behind his sternum, a tightening that felt less like fatigue and more like an invisible hand closing around his airway. By the time he collapsed in his kitchen, he was gasping for air that refused to fill his chest. The paramedics arrived quickly, but the sight of the oxygen mask and the IV line being threaded into his arm sent a jolt of pure horror through him. He remembers the cold steel of the needle, the rhythmic beep of the monitor, and the suffocating realization that his own lungs had turned against him. The illness was eventually managed, but the memory of that loss of control lingered long after the acute phase passed. The coherence between that original collapse and his current life was never in doubt; his body had learned, in the most violent way possible, to associate every drop of air with the steel of a needle and the hum of a medical machine. Over the following months, Caleb found himself bracing for the moment his chest would tighten again. What frightened him most was the sudden catch in his own breathing after a hurried sprint to catch the elevator. He would freeze, certain that the air was vanishing, his heart hammering against his ribs until the feeling passed. His body felt permanently wound, as though it were waiting for another collapse. When he caught himself gripping the edge of his desk at the office, palms sweating and breath shallow, he had come to believe he was simply keeping himself steady. He stopped taking the stairs. He avoided the gym entirely. The sight of treadmills coincided with a tightening in his throat, and he told himself he needed to conserve energy. His diet narrowed to precise portions of grilled chicken and rice. If he ate less, he reasoned, his body would remain manageable. He could control what went in, even if he could not control what went out. These adjustments did not feel like choices so much as necessities, woven into the same fabric as his constant vigilance. The database administrator’s open-plan floor became a landscape of monitored cues. When a senior developer coughed during a stand-up meeting, Caleb’s shoulders locked. He was certain the sound was a precursor to his own failure. He began wearing a high-collared shirt and kept his office door closed for hours, claiming he was optimizing query performance. He delegated the quarterly wellness screening to a colleague, convincing himself that a physical examination would only waste time. At home, the sight of the home blood pressure cuff on the counter made his stomach turn. He never unrolled it. Instead, he sat in the darkened study, waiting for the panic to pass. His body remained rigid. The shame of his own hesitation settled heavily in his chest alongside the fear, and the dread of medical equipment appeared whenever a promotional brochure landed on his kitchen counter. The negative emotions did not arrive in waves; they pooled steadily, a constant undercurrent that dictated his pace and his posture. At thirty-seven, the weight of these quiet restrictions had begun to fracture what remained of his routine. His divorce was finalized two years ago; his ex-wife had stopped asking why he flinched at the sound of an ambulance or why he refused to eat past his designated servings. He did not blame her, but he recognized that his own rigid perimeter had kept everyone at arm’s length. What finally brought him to the clinic was a Tuesday afternoon when a client’s presentation triggered a bout of coughing that left him gasping at his desk. The physical reaction was immediate and overwhelming, mirroring the collapse that had started it all. He realized he could no longer outrun the tension in his muscles or the dread that settled over him the moment a medical brochure appeared on a counter. He came to the intake expecting to be told he was broken, but what he was most hoping for was a way to let his lungs work again without fear, and to finally stop counting his meals like coordinates on a map.
